bib.title: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context", Lin, Maire, Belongie, Hays, Perona, Ramanan, Dollár, Zitnick. ECCV 2014, LNCS 8693, pp. 740–755.

COVERAGE: All 16 pages, 43,675 of 43,675 chars, references included. This is the 16-page ECCV camera-ready version. It has no appendix. For the category list, UIs and super-categories it points to the extended arXiv version (CoRR abs/1405.0312), which I did not read. Text extraction was clean.

CLAIMS
- claim: Dataset size is 91 "thing" categories, 2.5M labelled instances and 328k images. 82 of the categories have more than 5,000 instances.
  number: 91 / 2,500,000 / 328,000 / 82
  setup: The collection as it stood in 2014. The authors say segmentation is "still ongoing". The 91 is the proposed list.
  quote: "91 common object categories with 82 of them having more than 5,000 labeled instances, Fig. 6. In total the dataset has 2,500,000 labeled instances in 328,000 images." (p.741); "The completion of our final segmentation stage is still ongoing." (p.748)
- claim: COCO has more objects per image than ImageNet or PASCAL, and far fewer single-category images. Its objects are also smaller on average.
  number: 3.5 categories and 7.7 instances per image. ImageNet has 3.0 instances per image and PASCAL 2.3. 10% of COCO images contain one category, against more than 60% for the others.
  setup: For ImageNet they use the detection validation set. SUN has more objects per image (17+, counting objects and "stuff") but fewer instances overall.
  quote: "On average our dataset contains 3.5 categories and 7.7 instances per image... only 10% of the images in MS COCO have only one category per image, in comparison to over 60% of images containing a single object category in ImageNet and PASCAL VOC." (pp.748–749); "the average sizes of objects is smaller for both MS COCO and SUN." (p.749)
- claim: Images were chosen to be non-iconic. They came from Flickr, retrieved by searching for pairs of object categories or for a scene plus an object, never a single category in isolation.
  number: at most 5 photos per photographer within a short time window
  setup: The search used Flickr. Single-category searches with a filter for iconic images were a rare fallback.
  quote: "if we searched for pairwise combinations of object categories, such as 'dog + car' we found many more non-iconic images... We downloaded at most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window." (p.745)
- claim: Annotation ran on Amazon Mechanical Turk in three stages: hierarchical category labelling across 11 super-categories, instance spotting, and segmentation. The first two stages used 5 workers per image. Segmentation used 1 worker per instance, gated by a training task.
  number: 5 workers per image; 17,751 + 8,417 worker hours; more than 22 worker hours per 1,000 segmentations; about 1 in 3 workers passed training; about 60,000 worker hours in total
  setup: Spotting was capped at 10 instances of a category per image. Dense crowds were marked as one "do not care" segment that does not count in evaluation.
  quote: "ﬁve workers were asked to label each image... This stage took 17,751 worker hours" (p.746); "only about 1 in 3 workers passed the training stage" (p.747); "Utilizing around 60,000 worker hours" (p.753)
- claim: Label quality was checked against experts. The union of 5 AMT workers matches most experts on category recall. Expert recall itself was only 65–80%, because ground truth counts a category as present if any one expert labels it.
  number: 65%–80% expert recall; 70%–75% "generally sufficient"
  setup: Category-labelling stage only, against 7 experts who were co-authors. The authors treat precision as less important here because later stages remove false positives.
  quote: "5 AMT workers... achieves the same recall as most of the expert workers. Note that the expert labelers achieved between 65% and 80% recall." (p.748)
- claim: COCO is harder than PASCAL, and models trained on COCO lose less when tested across datasets.
  number: PASCAL-trained DPM scores 29.6 AP on PASCAL and 16.9 on COCO. The cross-dataset drop is 12.7 AP for the PASCAL-trained model and 7.7 AP for the COCO-trained one.
  setup: DPMv5, 20 PASCAL categories, a 55k-image subset, boxes derived from the masks. The split is 164k train, 82k val and 82k test, made by date and user with near-duplicates removed.
  quote: "average performance on MS COCO drops by nearly a factor of 2" (p.751); "The performance difference of the DPMv5-P models across the two datasets is 12.7 AP while the DPMv5-C models only have 7.7 AP difference." (p.751)

LIMITS:
- Coverage. COCO has "things" only, with no "stuff" (sky, grass). It uses entry-level categories only, with no fine-grained classes and no object parts.
- Captions. The paper has no captions. Sentence descriptions are listed only as future work: "full sentence written descriptions [51]" (p.753).
- Domains. Images are everyday Flickr photos of objects a 4-year-old would recognise. There is no text or OCR, no documents, charts or screenshots, and no medical or other specialised domains. The paper names none of these as gaps. They are absent by design.
- Annotation caps. Instances are capped at 10 per category in the spotting stage, and crowds are excluded from scoring, so counting and dense scenes are under-covered.
- Training value. The authors concede that hard non-iconic training images "may not always help" (p.751).
- Dated. The counts reflect a dataset still in progress, and the 82k test split was later re-split. Baselines are DPM only.

BUILDS ON:
- PASCAL VOC: Everingham et al., IJCV 2010. Also the source of the Flickr collection idea and the backwards-compatible categories.
- ImageNet: Deng et al., CVPR 2009.
- SUN: Xiao et al., CVPR 2010.
- Hierarchical multi-label annotation: Deng et al., CHI 2014.
- Segmentation UI from OpenSurfaces: Bell et al., SIGGRAPH 2013.
- Dataset bias and the cross-dataset metric: Torralba & Efros, CVPR 2011.
- Iconic images: Berg & Berg, CVPR 2009.
- Im2text: Ordonez et al., NIPS 2011.
- DPM: Felzenszwalb et al., PAMI 2010.

FIGURES (from the in-text captions; I did not run the figures.py captions script):
- Fig. 2, p.742: "Example of (a) iconic object images, (b) iconic scene images, and (c) non-iconic images." This is the best single picture of what "non-iconic" means and why COCO tests context.
- Alternative, Fig. 5, p.749: categories and instances per image, plus instance-size distributions, for COCO vs ImageNet, PASCAL and SUN.

PROBLEMS:
- Some words in the extraction are run together (for example "modelstestedonboth...", p.751).
- The Fig. 4 axis label is garbled ("MREVFRPSOHWHG", meaning "jobs completed").
- No embedded instructions were found.
